The reproductive biology of the rock cavy (Kerodon rupestris) has been documented through captive colony studies, providing detailed insights into its life-history strategy. Females typically produce litters of 1 to 2 pups [N_R_i = litters of 1 to 2 pups], and breeding occurs year-round under laboratory conditions. The maximum observed reproductive frequency is approximately 4.7 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 4.7 litters per year], a rate maintained when females are housed under thermal conditions approximating typical body temperature (38.2 °C [T = 38.2 °C]). Neonates are born in an advanced state of development, with a wet weight at birth of 76 grams [Wwb = 76 grams], a substantial mass that reflects a prolonged gestation period relative to other caviid rodents. This relatively large birth mass is thought to contribute to the pups' rapid locomotor development and early independence from maternal care.

Growth trajectories in Kerodon rupestris reveal a pattern of sustained mass gain from birth through adulthood. At a stable body temperature of 38.2 °C [T = 38.2 °C], weaning occurs approximately 35 days after birth [tx = approximately 35 days after birth], at which time the young animals have attained a wet weight of about 208 grams [Wwx = about 208 grams], representing a nearly threefold increase from their neonatal mass. This rapid pre-weaning growth is supported by the mother's milk and is followed by a continued, though decelerated, increase in body mass as the juveniles transition to a diet of leaves and browse. Ultimately, adult rock cavies reach an ultimate wet weight of approximately 1000 grams [Wwi = approximately 1000 grams], a body size that places them among the larger members of the family Caviidae. This asymptotic mass is typically achieved during the sub-adult stage, prior to the onset of reproductive maturity.

Under a stable core body temperature of 38.2 °C [T = 38.2 °C], sexual maturation in female rock cavies occurs at a relatively advanced age for a rodent of this size. The time since birth at puberty for females has been estimated at 151 days [tp = 151 days]. at a temperature of 38.2 °C [T = 38.2 °C]This extended juvenile period, lasting over five months, contrasts with the rapid early growth phase and is hypothesized to allow for the complete ossification of the skeleton and the development of complex social behaviors. Following the onset of first ovulation, females become capable of sustaining a pregnancy, which has been measured to last 75 days [tg = 75 days] at a temperature of 38.2 °C [T = 38.2 °C]. This gestation length, while considerably shorter than the 120 to 126 days sometimes cited in earlier literature, is consistent with the production of highly precocial offspring.

Basal metabolic measurements conducted under controlled laboratory settings provide a window into the energetic physiology of this species. At a core body temperature of 38.2 °C [T = 38.2 °C], the maximum basal metabolic rate recorded for adult rock cavies is 360.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 360.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This rate of oxygen consumption, reflecting the energetic cost of maintaining vital functions in a normothermic state, is relatively modest when standardized against the species' ultimate body mass of 1000 grams [Wwi = 1000 grams], a pattern consistent with the generally lower mass-specific metabolic rates observed in desert-adapted rodents. The rock cavy's natural habitat, the seasonally dry Caatinga of northeastern Brazil, imposes significant thermoregulatory demands, and the measured BMR may represent an adaptation to conserve energy during periods of thermal stress.

Longevity records from captive populations indicate that the rock cavy possesses a comparatively long lifespan for a hystricognath rodent of its size. The oldest documented individuals have survived for approximately 12.9 years [am = approximately 12.9 years] when maintained under conditions that include a stable body temperature of 38.2 °C [T = 38.2 °C]. This extended lifespan, approaching or exceeding 4,700 days, is coupled with a reproductive schedule that functions at a relatively slow pace compared to many other rodents of similar body mass, such as the guinea pig (Cavia porcellus), which typically lives only half as long. The demographic strategy of the rock cavy thus appears to prioritize adult survival and extended reproductive tenure over high annual fecundity, a life-history configuration that aligns with the species' occupation of a stable but resource-limited semiarid environment.
